title: Why AI tutors aren't transforming education
author: Thomas Arnett
summary: Thomas Arnett responds to the disappointing uptake of Khan Academy's Khanmigo, where only about 15 percent of students engaged regularly and a randomized trial found the tutor added little to the existing platform. He rejects both the skeptics who read this as proof that AI will never matter and the optimists who expect an imminent revolution. Using disruptive innovation theory, he argues that AI tutors plugged into conventional classrooms will deliver only marginal gains because learning depends on motivation, which is rooted in relationships, belonging, and status within a school community. He compares Khan Academy's fix to early factory managers who swapped steam engines for electric motors without redesigning the factory floor, a change that paid off only decades later. His prediction is that dramatic gains will come from new school models, such as microschools and hybrid or competency-based programs, that treat instruction and motivation as one design problem.
points: Khanmigo's thin engagement (about 15 percent regular use) shows that access to a capable AI tutor does not by itself produce learning.
Framing teaching as information transfer ignores motivation, which Arnett ties to relationships, belonging, and status, citing David Yeager's research on adolescent behavior.
The steam-to-electricity factory analogy shows that a better tool bolted onto an old structure yields little until the whole system is redesigned around it.
Both edtech optimists and skeptics watch conventional classrooms, when the real signal is in early-stage models at the margins of K-12 that rebuild schedules, grouping, and teacher roles.
School leaders should judge AI investments by whether they change the motivational structure around students, not only the quality of explanations.
quotes: A better AI tutor can explain fractions more clearly. It cannot make a student care about fractions. And caring—being embedded in a community and a set of relationships that make academic effort feel meaningful—turns out to be most of the problem.
Dramatic learning gains will require redesigning classrooms and schools with AI as one key piece in new learning models that rethink both instruction and student motivation.
Real learning takes effort, and students don’t put in that effort unless they are motivated to learn. But motivation doesn’t come just from making lessons fun or interesting.

But it is a better motor bolted to the same factory floor: Khanmigo remains a tutoring layer added on top of the conventional structure of a class, with the same schedule, the same grouping of students, and the same relationship between teacher, student, and content.

The optimists are watching the technology and assuming the transformation will come from the technology itself. The skeptics are watching the technology fail to transform student outcomes and concluding that the transformation isn’t coming.
My hypothesis is that any dramatic learning gains from AI will emerge from new models of schooling at the margins of K–12 education, not in conventional classrooms.

Then in August, a newly released randomized controlled trial delivered an even stronger verdict: for the students in the study, the AI tutor layered on top of Khan Academy’s existing practice platform added little beyond what the platform already did on its own.
